meta.title: Who really said "Hogamous, Higamous, Man is Polygamous, Higamous, Hogamous, Woman is Monagamous"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Dorothy Parker. The jingle first appeared in print in 1939, credited to Mrs. Amos Pinchot — who denied it. Parker's name was attached only in 1971.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hogamous, Higamous, Man is Polygamous, Higamous, Hogamous, Woman is Monagamous'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Dorothy Parker. First printed in 1939 crediting Mrs. Amos Pinchot, who denied it. The author is unknown; Parker's name appears only from 1971.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — an anonymous jingle
answer.authorDates: Credited over the years to Dorothy Parker (1893–1967), William James, Ogden Nash, Alice Duer Miller and Mrs. Amos Pinchot — none of them documented
answer.sourceLine: The verse first surfaces in a Cleveland Plain Dealer humour column of 23 November 1939, where Claire MacMurray tells it as a dream anecdote and credits Mrs. Amos Pinchot; by 1942 a psychology monograph was recording that Pinchot denied writing it and that the real author was “shrouded in anonymity.” Dorothy Parker’s name was not attached to the lines until 1971 — four years after her death — and the verse appears nowhere in her published work.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — an orphan jingle with no documented author, pinned on Parker decades after it was already in circulation.

source.heading: Where the jingle actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Cleveland Plain Dealer, 23 November 1939, p. 20 — credited there to Mrs. Amos Pinchot
Pinchot denied it; the author “appears to be shrouded in anonymity”
Not present — her real poem on the theme is ‘General Review of the Sex Situation’ (1926)

source.excerpt: As the story goes, the author dreamed one night that he had written a poem of such ultimate truth that he was immediately acclaimed to be the greatest poet and philosopher of all time. He immediately rose and scribbled it down, and the next morning found that he had written: Hogamus Higamus / Men are Polygamous / Higamus Hogamus / Women Monogamous.
trail: 23 November 1939 — the first known appearance: Claire MacMurray’s column “Thanksgiving Nightmare” in the Cleveland Plain Dealer tells the dream story and credits Mrs. Amos Pinchot, printing the verse as “Hogamus Higamus / Men are Polygamous / Higamus Hogamus / Women Monogamous” (Quote Investigator ↗). The Reader’s Digest reprinted it in May 1940 and spread it nationally.

1942 — James Grier Miller’s Unconsciousness retells the anecdote with the author unnamed, footnoting that Pinchot “denies any responsibility for it… and the true author appears to be shrouded in anonymity” (Internet Archive scan ↗).

1953 — Hans J. Eysenck’s Uses and Abuses of Psychology is the first place Quote Investigator finds William James named, calling it the quatrain James “wrote down during a drug-induced dream” — more than four decades after James died in 1910 (Quote Investigator ↗).

1971 — a developmental-psychology textbook is the earliest source Quote Investigator finds assigning the verse to Dorothy Parker, retelling the same dream story with her in the starring role (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: From James Grier Miller’s Unconsciousness (1942), pp. 131–132. The attached footnote reads: “Mrs. Amos Pinchot has repeatedly been incorrectly said to have been the author of this quatrain. She denies any responsibility for it, however, and the true author appears to be shrouded in anonymity.” Note the early spelling and the plural “Men are” — the familiar “Man is polygamous” wording is a later mutation.

source.rightsNote: No author and no first publication can be established for this wording, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. Its earliest known printing — Claire MacMurray’s Cleveland Plain Dealer column of 23 November 1939 — is itself well after 1930 and would carry its own rights; by contrast, Dorothy Parker’s genuine poem on the same theme, from Enough Rope (1926), is in the public domain and freely readable at Project Gutenberg ↗.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: Why the jingle sounds like Dorothy Parker
author.bio: Dorothy Parker made her name at Vanity Fair and The New Yorker and at the Algonquin Round Table, writing short, savage, perfectly rhymed verse about love and disappointment. Her first collection, Enough Rope (Boni & Liveright, 1926), contains a poem that says almost exactly what the “Hogamous” jingle says — “General Review of the Sex Situation,” which opens “Woman wants monogamy; / Man delights in novelty.” That real poem is very likely why an anonymous piece of doggerel on the same theme drifted onto her name; the doggerel itself is not in her books.

Author unknown. Dorothy Parker’s name was not attached until 1971.

misattribution.heading: Five authors, no evidence
misattribution.intro: This is a rare case where the quote arrived first and the famous names arrived afterwards. Every candidate was proposed years or decades after the verse was already circulating in print, and not one attribution comes with a manuscript, a book, a letter or a witness.

items.why: The earliest Parker credit Quote Investigator located is a 1971 developmental-psychology textbook — published after her death in 1967 and decades after the verse was in print (Quote Investigator ↗). Tony Percy, who investigated the verse for Verbatim, concluded that although it “certainly has a Parkerian feel to it… no trace of ‘Hogamous’ appears in Parker’s works” (Verbatim, reprinted at Coldspur ↗). Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page carries no entry for it in any section.

The famous tale — James inhales laughing gas, scrawls the secret of the universe, wakes to find this doggerel — is the most repeated version and the least supported. Quote Investigator’s earliest James attribution is Hans Eysenck’s in 1953, and the nitrous-oxide detail only turns up in Robert S. De Ropp’s The Master Game in 1968. James died in 1910, and Quote Investigator finds “no substantive evidence” that he wrote it (Quote Investigator ↗).

Quote Investigator suggests the Nash credit may stem from confusion with a real 1942 Nash poem that plays on deliberately misspelt rhymes — “Why does the Pygmy / Indulge in polygmy?… If he sticks to monogmy / A Pygmy’s a hogmy” — which is a different piece of verse entirely (Quote Investigator ↗).

She is the one candidate named in the earliest citation, in 1939, and she is also the only one on record refusing the credit: a 1942 footnote states she “denies any responsibility for it” (Unconsciousness, 1942 ↗).

A New York Times report of 12 May 1946 on a United Nations debate about equal rights in marriage quoted the verse as “ascribed by some experts” to Alice Duer Miller — a passing aside with no supporting reference, and one that did not stick (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who wrote it. Quote Investigator’s verdict is that “the identity of the author remains uncertain today, but well-known wits Ogden Nash and Dorothy Parker are unlikely” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: The joke was never about who said it
lead: The jingle began life as a punchline, not a quotation. In its earliest printed form it is the payoff of a small comic story: a woman dreams she has written a poem so profound it will make her the greatest philosopher who ever lived, scrambles out of bed to write it down, and finds this in the morning. The verse is supposed to be a let-down — that is the whole gag — which is exactly why it needed no author to work.

The famous names arrived later, and each one made the anecdote better. William James inhaling nitrous oxide is a funnier story than an anonymous lady having a dream; Dorothy Parker waking up to it is funnier still. What none of these versions ever acquired was a source. The verse had been in print for more than a decade before James’s name appeared on it, and for over thirty years before Parker’s did.
context.detailsSummary: The wording drifted too — and Parker’s real poem on the subject
detailsBody: Parker’s name may have stuck because she had already published the same thought properly. “General Review of the Sex Situation,” from Enough Rope (1926), runs: “Woman wants monogamy; / Man delights in novelty. / Love is woman’s moon and sun; / Man has other forms of fun…” Same argument, same brevity, real authorship — and it is in the public domain, unlike the orphan jingle, whose status cannot be determined at all.

The wording has also drifted. The 1939 and 1942 texts read “Hogamus Higamus / Men are Polygamous”; a 1946 anthology introduced the doubled-g “Hoggamus, higgamus”; and the singular “Man is polygamous… Woman is monagamous” form now most often quoted is a later variant. Any page that gives you a confident author and a confident wording is giving you more certainty than the record supports.
context.pull: The joke only works if the poem is a disappointment. Attaching a genius to it was a later improvement.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest citation is the Cleveland Plain Dealer, 23 November 1939, 'Thanksgiving Nightmare' by Claire MacMurray, p. 20 col. 3, crediting Mrs. Amos Pinchot; Reader's Digest reprinted it May 1940; a 1942 cite records Pinchot's denial; Eysenck (1953) is the first to name William James, who died in 1910; De Ropp (1968) adds the nitrous oxide; a 1971 developmental-psychology textbook is the first Dorothy Parker credit; the New York Times of 12 May 1946 named Alice Duer Miller; Ogden Nash's 1942 'Pygmy/polygmy' poem may explain the Nash credit; QI concludes the author 'remains uncertain today, but well-known wits Ogden Nash and Dorothy Parker are unlikely'.

Tony Percy's Verbatim study states the quatrain 'certainly has a Parkerian feel to it' but that 'no trace of "Hogamous" appears in Parker's works. Thus there is a good chance that the whole anecdote is apocryphal.' It also quotes Parker's real poem 'General Review of the Sex Situation' and discusses Bertrand Russell as a possible origin of the William James anecdote.

James Grier Miller, Unconsciousness (John Wiley & Sons, 1942), pp. 131-132, prints the anecdote with the author unnamed and footnote 69 reading: 'Mrs. Amos Pinchot has repeatedly been incorrectly said to have been the author of this quatrain. She denies any responsibility for it, however, and the true author appears to be shrouded in anonymity.' The verse there reads 'Hogamus Higamus / Men are Polygamous / Higamus Hogamus / Women Monogamous.' Verified in the scanned OCR text of this Internet Archive item, whose metadata gives the title, author, publisher and 1942 date.

The full text of Dorothy Parker's Enough Rope (Boni & Liveright, New York, 1926; first printing December 1926) contains 'General Review of the Sex Situation' beginning 'Woman wants monogamy; / Man delights in novelty.' A search of the complete text returns zero occurrences of 'hogam' or 'higam'.
Poets.org prints 'General Review of the Sex Situation' in full and sources it to Enough Rope (Boni & Liveright, 1926) by Dorothy Parker, noting the poem is in the public domain.

Wikiquote's Dorothy Parker page gives her dates as August 22, 1893 - June 7, 1967 and contains no entry for the 'Hogamous/Higamous' verse in any section (zero occurrences of 'ogamus' or 'ogamous' in the page's raw wikitext).
